title: A Funeral Song for Judah's Kings
overview: Ezekiel mourns the last kings of Judah, picturing them first as captured lions and then as a proud vine torn up and burned.

parts.label: The lioness and her cubs (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Ezekiel is told to mourn Judah's royal family, called here the princes of Israel, as if grieving at their graveside. The mother lioness probably stands for Judah or its royal house, since the lion was an old symbol of Judah, though some think she is a particular queen mother.

parts.label: First cub taken to Egypt (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: This is almost certainly King Jehoahaz, who ruled only three months before Egypt's Pharaoh took him away in chains around 609 BC. The pit and hooks come from how wild animals were trapped, and captives were sometimes led the same way.

parts.label: Second cub caged for Babylon (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: Scholars are unsure which king this is: Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin or Zedekiah have all been suggested, with Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC, a common view. His violent roaring pictures harsh rule, and the silenced roar means his reign ended in captivity.

parts.label: The proud vine (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: The picture changes to a vine planted by plenty of water, meaning Judah in a good land. Its strong branches, fit to be a ruler's staff, stand for the kings who once grew from it.

parts.label: Uprooted and dried out (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: The vine is torn up in anger, scorched by the hot desert east wind and replanted in dry ground. This pictures Babylon destroying the kingdom and the people living in exile.

parts.label: Fire from its own branch (v. 14)
parts.note: The fire starting from one of its own branches likely points to King Zedekiah, whose revolt against Babylon brought final ruin, so no king's staff was left. Christians later read this loss alongside promises of a future king from David's family, whom they see in Jesus.

think: When a family or a nation loses something it once took pride in, how much of that loss comes from outside forces and how much from its own choices?
